en: The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having completed his almsround through the city in due order, he returned to his original place.
When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.

At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One,
how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
"How does one subdue the mind?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Subhūti! It is as you have said:
"The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should abide in this manner and thus subdue their minds."
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way:

‘May I cause every kind of living being—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—to enter into nirvāṇa without remainder and bring them to liberation.’”
"In this way, although he brings immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva has the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything in relation to phenomena; that is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor should they dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental objects when practicing giving.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should give in this way, not dwelling upon signs. Why is that?
"If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit and virtue cannot be measured or conceived.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can the eastern expanse of space be measured? “No, World-Honored One. “Subhūti!”
“Can the empty space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured? “No, World-Honored One. “Subhūti!”
When a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit is likewise inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide in accordance with what has been taught.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks. Why is this? Because..."
"The physical marks described by the Tathāgata are, in truth, not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever marks there may be, they are all illusory; [they are empty]."
“If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Are there any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus."

In the five hundred years following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses and take them as truth. You should know that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas.
"Subhūti, as for those who hear these phrases and give rise to even a single thought of pure faith,
the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that all such sentient beings shall obtain immeasurable merit."
Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.
They have no notion of dharmas, nor do they have any notion of non-dharmas.
Why is this? If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they are then attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they take up the signs of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Why is this? If one grasps at the signs of what is not the Dharma, one is attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has often said:
"O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the simile of the raft; even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
“Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied,
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,’ nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could preach.”
Why is this? All the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. Why is that?
"All worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-activity (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"If a person were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? Because that merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says the merit is great.
"If, moreover, there should be someone who receives, upholds, and even recites as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it for others, their merit would surpass that."
Why is this? Subhūti!
All Buddhas and the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas all emerge from this sūtra.
Subhūti! What are called the Buddha-dharmas are not, in fact, Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Does a stream-enterer have the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
A Srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream,' yet there is nothing entered; they do not enter form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, or dharmas—this is called a Srotāpanna."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a sakṛdāgāmin have the thought, ‘I have attained the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin’?”
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One! Why is this so?"
"One who returns once more is called a Sakṛdāgāmin; yet in reality there is no coming or going, and thus he is named a Sakṛdāgāmin.
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can an Anāgāmin have the thought, ‘I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Anāgāmin is called "one who does not come," yet in reality there is no coming; therefore, he is named Anāgāmin. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Does an Arhat have the thought, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Because, in reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat'."
World-Honored One!
If an Arhat were to have this thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," he would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha has declared that among all people, I am foremost in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-Contention, and that I am the foremost Arhat free from desire.
Yet, I do not harbor such a thought:”
"I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One!
If I had thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship," then the World-Honored One would not have said that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
"Because Subhūti has in reality nothing to practice, he is called 'Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain anything regarding the Dharma?
"World-Honored One,
when the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields?”
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not adornment; it is called 'adornment' only by name."

"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on forms; they should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. They should give rise to that mind by dwelling nowhere."
“Subhūti! Suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be great?”
Subhūti said: “It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One! Why is this so?”
“The Buddha has said that what is not a body is called the ‘great body. Subhūti,
suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River— what do you think?”
“Are all these Ganges rivers many? Subhūti replied,
“Very many, World-Honored One!”
“Yet even the Ganges Rivers themselves are already countless, how much more so their sands.
“Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth:

if there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and used them for giving, would they gain much merit?”
Subhūti said: “Very much, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a good man or good woman, from within this sutra, should even accept and uphold as few as four lines of verse and explain them to others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha; how much more so for one who can fully receive, uphold, read, and recite it?"
Subhūti! You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. Wherever this sutra resides, there is a Buddha, or a respected disciple.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this sutra be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The name of this sutra is 'Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā'."
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that? Subhūti!
The Buddha said that Prajñāpāramitā is not Prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti,
what do you think?
“Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“The Tathāgata has nothing to teach. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
“Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied,
“Very many, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti! Those atoms, the Tathāgata has said, are not atoms; they are called ‘atoms.
The world-system, the Tathāgata has said, is not a world-system; it is called a ‘world-system.’”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? Because..."
“The Tathāgata speaks of the thirty-two marks, yet these are non-marks; they are called the ‘thirty-two marks.
Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, with as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practiced giving;”
"Furthermore, if there should be a person who, from within this sutra, even receives and upholds as few as four lines of verse and explains them to others, their merit would be exceedingly great.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this teaching of the sutra, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this; from my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this.
World-Honored One!

If there are further people who hear this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they will give rise to the mark of reality; you should know that such persons have accomplished the foremost and most rare merit.
“World-Honored One!
This true mark is, in fact, no mark; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘true mark.
World-Honored One!”

For me now to hear such a sutra as this and to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it is not difficult; however, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such persons would be the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because this person has no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, and no notion of a life-span. Why is that so?
The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks.
Why is this? Because one who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is truly rare.”
Why is this? Subhūti, what the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not a foremost pāramitā; it is designated as the foremost pāramitā.
Subhūti! The perfection of patience, the Tathāgata says, is not the perfection of patience. Why is that?
Subhūti! When I was formerly dismembered by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span.

Why is this? If, when my body was being dismembered limb by limb in the past, I had harbored any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

Subhūti! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience; throughout those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by relinquishing all marks. One should not give rise to the mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
If the mind has a dwelling place, then it is not truly dwelling.
Therefore, the Buddha said that the bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving. "Subhūti!..."
A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner.
The Tathāgata has said:
"All marks are, in fact, no-marks."
Furthermore, it is said:
"All sentient beings are, in fact, not sentient beings. Subhūti!
The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks as it is, one who does not speak deceptively, and one who does not speak otherwise. "Subhūti!..."
The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata— this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.
"If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who, when the sun shines brightly, sees all manner of forms. Subhūti!"

In a future age, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the Tathāgata, with the wisdom of a Buddha, will fully know these people and fully see these people; they shall all achieve immeasurable and boundless merit.

“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, gave as many bodies in alms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and during the middle part of the day again gave as many bodies in alms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and during the latter part of the day likewise gave as many bodies in alms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—giving their bodies in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas;

yet if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, did not oppose it with a mind of faith, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former, let alone one who copies it, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, or explains it to others.”
“Subhūti! To speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this to others, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all; they shall all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit. Such persons as these shall carry upon their shoulders the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span; they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra for others.
“Subhūti! Wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras;
you should know that such a place is itself a stupa. Everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it, scattering various flowers and incense upon that spot.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If good men or good women who uphold, read, and recite this sutra are treated with contempt by others, their karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are instead extinguished by virtue of being so treated by others in the present life. They shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, never letting any pass in vain.

If there should be someone in the future final age who can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain will not be matched by even a hundredth part of the merit I gained from making offerings to those Buddhas; it does not even reach a thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by calculation or analogy.”

“Subhūti! If I were to describe in full the merit obtained by good sons and good daughters who, in the final age, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and, filled with doubt, would not believe it.”
“Subhūti! You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When a good man or a good woman resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should they abide?
How should they subdue their minds?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I shall bring all sentient beings to final liberation (*parinirvāṇa*). "
"Having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, there is not a single sentient being who has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
If a bodhisattva has the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti!
"In reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma by which he attained anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi?
“No, World-Honored One.”
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
If there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara would not have granted me this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
"Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for this reason the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me the prediction, saying:
'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.'"
Why is this? The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas.
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Tathāgata has attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi," [it would be a misconception].
In truth, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! Regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, therein is neither reality nor unreality; for this reason, the Tathāgata says:
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is not all dharmas; it is therefore called "all dharmas."
“Subhūti, it is as if,
for example, a human body were long and large. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of the human body as being long and large, it is not actually a large body; it is merely designated as a ‘large body. “Subhūti!
A bodhisattva is also like this: if they should say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then they are not called a bodhisattva. Why is that?
Subhūti! In reality, there is no dharma that can be called a "bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"All dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely designated as "adornment. Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River what the Buddha calls 'sand'? "Yes, World-Honored One."
“The Tathāgata says they are sand. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River; and suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would these not be very numerous?
“Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds possessed by all sentient beings.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are non-minds; it is precisely for this reason that they are called "minds. Why is that so?
Subhūti! The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. Subhūti!
What do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?
"So it is, World-Honored One!
By these causes and conditions, this person gains exceedingly great merit. "Subhūti!"
If merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains much merit;
because merit is non-substantial, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit. "Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected physical body? "No, World-Honored One."
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the body of perfect form. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the body of perfect form is itself not a body of perfect form; it is merely designated as the "body of perfect form."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks?”
"No, World-Honored One! One should not see the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this? Because..."
“The Tathāgata speaks of the perfection of all marks, yet this is not perfection; it is merely called the perfection of all marks.
“Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has the thought: ‘I shall preach some dharma.’”
Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this?
If anyone says, "The Tathāgata has preached a dharma," they slander the Buddha, for they fail to understand what I have taught.
"Subhūti! One who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! They are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
"Subhūti! As for 'sentient beings, sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as 'sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained? “It is so, it is so!”
Subhūti! In my Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; it is for this reason that it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, without high or low; it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By practicing all wholesome dharmas without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Subhūti! Those things called wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata has said they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas. Subhūti!
If someone were to take all the Sumeru Kings and such heaps of the seven treasures as exist within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift;

and if another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even so much as a four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the former merit would not equal one hundredth part of the latter, nor one part in a hundred-thousand-million-billion, nor could it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor.
“Subhūti, what do you think? You should not suppose that the Tathāgata thinks thus:”
"Subhūti, do not harbor such a thought as 'I shall deliver sentient beings.'"

Why is this? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti! When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, he does not speak of a self; yet ordinary people imagine there is a self. Subhūti!
"Ordinary persons, the Tathāgata says, are not ordinary persons. Subhūti,
what do you think?"
“Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is!”
"One should contemplate the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would be the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one sees me by form, Or seeks me by sound,..."
Such people follow a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Subhūti, if you should have this thought:
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection.
Do not harbor such a thought.”
“The Tathāgata does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection.
“Subhūti! If you should have this thought:”
"One who has set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi speaks of the characteristic of the annihilation and cessation of all dharmas.
Do not entertain such a thought. Why is this?
"One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the mark of annihilation regarding phenomena.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva were to give in charity the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;..."
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is another person who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains patience, this bodhisattva surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva. Subhūti!
"Because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that a bodhisattva does not receive merit?
"Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with craving; for this reason, it is said that they do not receive merit."
“Subhūti, if anyone were to say,
‘The Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down,’ that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. "Subhūti!..."
"If a good man or a good woman were to grind this trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that multitude of atoms be numerous?"
“Very many, World-Honored One! Why is this?
If these multitudes of atoms were substantially existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as ‘multitudes of atoms.’”
Why is this? The Buddha spoke of a multitude of atoms, yet they are not a multitude of atoms; they are called a "multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One!
The "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; it is merely designated as a "world.
Why is this? If a world were truly existent, it would be a unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).
“The Tathāgata speaks of a ‘unified whole,’ yet it is not a unified whole; it is merely called a ‘unified whole.
Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is ineffable; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.”
“Subhūti! If someone were to say, ‘The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span,’ Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Does this person understand the meaning of what I have taught?
"World-Honored One!"
This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this?

When the World-Honored One speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."

“Subhūti! Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus, without giving rise to the notion of phenomena.”
Subhūti! That which is called the "characteristic of dharmas" is, according to the Tathāgata, not a characteristic of dharmas; it is merely designated as the "characteristic of dharmas. Subhūti!

If someone were to take seven treasures filling immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds and offer them as a gift, and if there were a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and takes up even as little as a four-line verse from this sutra—upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others—their merit would surpass that of the former.
How does one expound the teaching for others?
By not grasping at appearances, remaining as suchness, unmoving. Why is this?
"All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as all the devas, humans, and asuras in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mantra of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: Namo bhagavatyai prajñāpāramitāyai | Oṃ ilīti iśrī śuludha viśaye viśaye svāhā || Buddha!
